cards.title: Skin — face
cards.sub: Hydration, barrier protection, and cell turnover are the core goals

rows.text: Gentle pH-balanced cleanser morning and evening; moisturizer with ceramides or hyaluronic acid; SPF 30+ any time outdoors
Chemical exfoliant 1–2x (AHA or BHA — gentler and more effective than physical scrubs); eye cream if addressing fine lines
Retinol or retinoid treatment (start low, 0.025–0.05%) — the most evidence-backed ingredient for collagen and skin aging
Dermatologist visit for full skin check — note any new, changing, or asymmetric spots

cards.title: Skin — body
cards.sub: Neglected relative to face care — same principles apply

rows.text: Moisturize immediately after shower while skin is damp (seals hydration); body oil or lotion with shea or glycerin
Dry brushing or exfoliating scrub on legs, arms, back — promotes circulation and removes dead skin buildup
Full-body mole check using the ABCDE rule: Asymmetry, Border, Color, Diameter >6mm, Evolution — photograph to track changes over time
Full-body skin check with dermatologist; more frequent if many moles or family history of melanoma

cards.title: Feet
cards.sub: High-load, high-neglect — issues compound quickly without maintenance

rows.text: Foot roller or lacrosse ball (2–3 min/foot); rich foot cream on heels and dry areas before bed
Pumice stone on damp skin; check between toes for dryness or fungal signs; toe splay and intrinsic foot exercises
Deep callus care or pedicure; nail trim straight across to prevent ingrowth
Assess footwear wear patterns and replace worn athletic shoes — worn-out soles silently degrade gait and joint loading

cards.title: Hands & nails
cards.sub: Hands age visibly — hydration and sun protection matter here too

rows.text: Hand cream after washing (frequent washing strips skin); SPF on hands if outdoors — one of the fastest-aging areas
Nail trim and filing; cuticle oil to prevent cracking and hangnails; check nails for color or texture changes
Note any changes in nail ridging, pitting, or discoloration — can indicate thyroid, iron, or fungal issues worth investigating

cards.title: Hair & scalp
cards.sub: Scalp health underlies hair health — most hair concerns start at the root

rows.text: 2-min scalp massage (fingertips, not nails) — stimulates follicle circulation; rosemary oil application has clinical support for hair density
Shampoo 2–3x depending on activity level; conditioner on lengths; check hairline and part for density changes
Scalp oil treatment overnight (jojoba, rosemary, or castor); photograph hairline year-over-year to detect gradual changes
Discuss hair thinning with dermatologist if progressing — early intervention is far more effective than late-stage treatment

cards.title: Eyes
cards.sub: Screen fatigue and dry eye are the dominant concerns in desk workers

rows.text: Preservative-free lubricating drops as needed; 20-20-20 rule — every 20 min, look 20 ft away for 20 sec; warm screen tone (night shift mode) reduces strain
Warm compress on eyelids 5 min — clears meibomian glands and improves tear film quality, reducing chronic dry eye
Comprehensive eye exam including dilated retinal check; note any new floaters or flashes immediately — warrants same-day evaluation

cards.title: Teeth & gums
cards.sub: Oral health is a direct predictor of cardiovascular and metabolic health

rows.text: Brush 2x with soft bristle brush (2 min); floss once daily; tongue scraper to reduce oral bacteria
Oil pulling with coconut oil (10–15 min) — supports reduction in gingival bacteria and plaque; check gum line for recession
Professional cleaning every 6 months; discuss night guard if any jaw tension, grinding, or morning headaches

cards.title: Ears
cards.sub: Self-cleaning system — over-intervention is the most common mistake

rows.text: Clean outer ear with damp cloth only — no cotton swabs inside canal; use hearing protection at concerts, power tools, or loud events
Hydrogen peroxide drops if fullness or buildup (1–2 drops, tilt and drain); monitor headphone volume — stay under 80% for extended use
Hearing test every 2–3 years from age 40; see ENT promptly for any tinnitus, muffling, or sudden change

cards.title: Nasal & sinus
cards.sub: Dry air and allergens are the main culprits — simple interventions help a lot

rows.text: Bedroom humidifier (45–55% humidity); saline nasal spray in dry or allergy-heavy seasons
Neti pot or Navage nasal irrigation — especially during allergy season; clean device thoroughly between uses
Track allergy patterns year to year; consider allergy testing if recurring sinus congestion is affecting sleep quality

cards.title: Posture & spine
cards.sub: Desk work is the single biggest structural threat in this lifestyle

rows.text: Alternate sit/stand every 45–60 min; 5-min thoracic opener before and after desk sessions (doorway stretch, cat-cow, band pull-aparts)
Dead hang from pull-up bar (30–60 sec) for spinal decompression; dedicated hip flexor stretch series — sitting shortens these significantly
Audit workstation — monitor height, chair depth, keyboard angle; side-profile photo to check for head-forward posture drift
Sports medicine or PT check-in to catch postural asymmetries before they become structural problems

cards.title: Mobility & flexibility
cards.sub: Flexibility is the first fitness quality lost after 35 without deliberate maintenance

rows.text: 10-min morning mobility flow targeting hips, thoracic spine, ankles, and wrists — the highest-ROI daily habit at this age
Dedicated yoga or deep stretch session (30+ min); posterior chain focus — hamstrings, glutes, piriformis tend to be chronically tight in desk workers
Benchmark range of motion — hip hinge, squat depth, shoulder flexion, thoracic rotation; note any regression early

cards.title: Joints & tendons
cards.sub: Tendons adapt 10x slower than muscle — the most under-managed tissue in active people

rows.text: Joint warm-up before any training — wrist circles, shoulder CARs, hip 90/90; do not skip as you age
Eccentric loading work (slow negatives on pull-ups, Nordic curls, single-leg calf raises) — gold standard for tendon health
Collagen supplement with vitamin C (10–15g, 30–45 min pre-workout) — supports tendon collagen synthesis when timed this way
Knee, shoulder, and elbow check — note crepitus or pain onset patterns before they progress to structural damage

cards.title: Pelvic floor & core
cards.sub: Foundational for spine health, organ support, and longevity — relevant to all genders

rows.text: Diaphragmatic breathing (360° rib expansion, not chest) — resets pelvic floor and core coordination; effective during desk work
Anti-rotation core work — dead bug, bird dog, pallof press — builds spinal stability more effectively than crunches or sit-ups
Pelvic floor PT baseline assessment — especially post-partum for women; also relevant for anyone with history of heavy lifting or high-impact sport

cards.title: Sleep
cards.sub: The most powerful recovery and anti-aging tool available — chronically undervalued

rows.text: Consistent wake time (even weekends); blackout curtains or sleep mask; cool room (65–68°F); no screens 30 min before bed
Review sleep quality patterns if tracking — alcohol, late meals, and stress are the top three disruptors in this life stage
Discuss sleep quality honestly with your doctor; consider a sleep study if snoring, or waking unrefreshed despite adequate hours

cards.title: Gut health
cards.sub: A diverse, plant-rich diet is already optimal — maintain and monitor

rows.text: Aim for 30+ plant species per week; include fermented foods regularly — kimchi, sauerkraut, tempeh, yogurt, kefir
Note digestion signals — bloating, regularity, and energy after meals are real gut health indicators
First colonoscopy at 45 (or earlier with family history); microbiome test if chronic fatigue or mood issues are present

cards.title: Hormonal & metabolic
cards.sub: Testosterone, estrogen, thyroid, and insulin sensitivity all shift meaningfully around 40

rows.text: Resistance training sessions (even 20–30 min) are the most powerful lever for preserving hormone balance and muscle mass at this age
Track body composition trends — waist-to-height ratio is a more meaningful metabolic marker than weight alone
Full panel: sex hormones (total + free), thyroid (TSH, T3, T4), fasting glucose, HbA1c, vitamin D, iron, and full micronutrient profile

cards.title: Cardiovascular
cards.sub: Zone 2 aerobic capacity is the strongest single predictor of longevity

rows.text: 150 min Zone 2 cardio (conversational pace, nasal breathing) — cycling, hiking, and brisk walking all qualify; plus 1–2 higher-intensity sessions
Note resting heart rate trend — gradual improvement indicates improving fitness; rising baseline is an early stress or illness signal
Blood pressure check; lipid panel; VO2 max test at 40 as a longevity baseline; EKG if any family history of cardiac events

cards.title: Nutrition optimization
cards.sub: Flexitarian diet is strong — small strategic additions close the remaining gaps

rows.text: Creatine monohydrate (3–5g) — strong evidence for muscle preservation, cognitive function, and recovery in 40+ adults regardless of diet type
Adequate protein — 0.7–1g per lb of bodyweight; plant sources require intentional combining to hit complete amino acid profiles
Annual blood panel already in place — let results drive supplementation; adjust year-to-year based on documented trends

cards.title: Stress & nervous system
cards.sub: Chronic stress silently accelerates most forms of physical and cognitive aging

rows.text: Physiological sigh (double inhale through nose, long slow exhale) — fastest evidence-based nervous system downregulation; 2–3 cycles is enough
One genuine recovery activity — sauna, nature walk, breathwork, or meditation; passive screen time does not qualify as nervous system recovery
Honest stress audit; cortisol saliva panel if chronic fatigue or stubborn weight gain persists despite good diet and exercise habits

cards.title: Skin cancer checks
cards.sub: Most treatable when caught early — self-monitoring bridges annual derm visits

rows.text: Full-body self-check using ABCDE rule — Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter >6mm, Evolution; use a mirror or partner for back and scalp
Photograph any suspicious or existing moles with consistent lighting — side-by-side comparison reveals evolution invisible in single checks
Full-body dermatologist skin check annually; more frequently with fair skin, many moles, significant UV history, or family history of melanoma

cards.title: Breast health
cards.sub: Self-familiarity is the foundation of early detection

rows.text: Breast self-exam 5–7 days after period ends (when tissue is least dense); look and feel for lumps, skin dimpling, nipple changes, or asymmetry
Clinical breast exam at each annual well-woman visit; discuss mammogram start date with doctor — guidelines vary (40–45 depending on risk factors)

cards.title: Testicular health
cards.sub: Peak incidence in 20s–40s — most curable cancer when found early

rows.text: Self-exam after a warm shower (relaxed tissue); roll each testicle gently between fingers — check for any hard lump, swelling, heaviness, or size change
Discuss prostate health with doctor at 40; PSA baseline at 40–45 especially with family history; prostate exam timeline depends on individual risk profile

cards.title: Colorectal health
cards.sub: Third most common cancer — highly preventable with screening

rows.text: High-fiber, plant-diverse diet is already protective — continue prioritizing legumes, whole grains, and cruciferous vegetables
Note any sustained changes in bowel habits, stool color (dark/black or blood), or unexplained fatigue — worth flagging early
First colonoscopy at 45; at 40 with family history of colorectal cancer; stool DNA test (Cologuard) is an option between scopes

cards.title: Cervical health
cards.sub: Highly preventable — regular screening catches pre-cancerous changes

rows.text: Pap smear every 3 years (ages 21–65); co-test with HPV every 5 years (ages 30–65) is an alternative; discuss scheduling with OB-GYN
Well-woman visit annually regardless of Pap schedule — covers pelvic exam, STI screening if relevant, and general reproductive health

cards.title: General annual screenings
cards.sub: Baseline checks that apply to all adults entering their 40s

rows.text: Blood pressure, resting heart rate, fasting glucose, HbA1c, full lipid panel, liver enzymes, kidney function (eGFR, creatinine)
Full micronutrient and hormone panel — document year-over-year trends, not just single-point snapshots
Dental cleaning x2/year; eye exam x1/year; hearing test every 2–3 years; bone density (DEXA) scan baseline at 40–45

cards.title: Brain & cognition
cards.sub: Processing speed peaks at ~35 — neuroplasticity and maintenance are the goals from here

rows.text: Novel learning (language, instrument, new skill domains) — novelty is the primary driver of neuroplasticity; physical exercise is the #1 evidence-based cognitive maintenance tool
Meaningful social connection beyond family — social isolation is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for cognitive decline and dementia
Note any subjective changes in word retrieval, memory, or focus — establishing a personal baseline now makes future comparison meaningful

cards.title: Mental & emotional health
cards.sub: Career + family stress is a well-documented inflection point for long-term mental health

rows.text: Even 10 min of unstructured solitude (walk, sit outside, no phone) — small consistent decompression matters more than occasional big resets
One activity purely for personal enjoyment, outside of family and work obligation; protect it as a non-negotiable
Honest mental health check-in — with a therapist, a trusted partner, or both; normalize it as maintenance, not crisis response
